papers.title: Performance Guarantees for Permissionless Lending
papers.abstract: We propose a lending protocol with far fewer risks than existing pool-based lending protocols (e.g., Aave, Compound). In our protocol, lenders and borrowers embody the spirit of decentralization by making competing interest-rate offers, resulting in the discovery of the prevailing interest rate through t\^atonnement-like dynamics as opposed to taking rates partly determined by a central authority (e.g., Aave, Federal Reserve). We eliminate the risk of manipulation by creating loans with a fixed interest rate throughout the loan---like US Treasury bills. In particular, we further derive performance guarantees probabilities of repayment shortfall and liquidation by modeling the value of the collateral as a random walk, thus allowing participants to more efficiently manage their risk. To do so, we use characteristic functions and Fourier inversion to derive exact integral representations of the liquidation and repayment shortfall probabilities under the most general assumptions. We illustrate empirically this method by using Bitcoin as collateral and fitting its historical prices to Gaussian, Student-$t$, and symmetric stable Paretian distributions.

papers.title: Discovering and Reasoning of Causality in the Hidden World with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Revealing hidden causal variables alongside the underlying causal mechanisms is essential to the development of science. Despite the progress in the past decades, existing practice in causal discovery (CD) heavily relies on high-quality measured variables, which are usually given by human experts. In fact, the lack of well-defined high-level variables behind unstructured data has been a longstanding roadblock to a broader real-world application of CD. This procedure can naturally benefit from an automated process that can suggest potential hidden variables in the system. Interestingly, Large language models (LLMs) are trained on massive observations of the world and have demonstrated great capability in processing unstructured data. To leverage the power of LLMs, we develop a new framework termed Causal representatiOn AssistanT (COAT) that incorporates the rich world knowledge of LLMs to propose useful measured variables for CD with respect to high-value target variables on their paired unstructured data. Instead of directly inferring causality with LLMs, COAT constructs feedback from intermediate CD results to LLMs to refine the proposed variables. Given the target variable and the paired unstructured data, we first develop COAT-MB that leverages the predictivity of the proposed variables to iteratively uncover the Markov Blanket of the target variable. Built upon COAT-MB, COAT-PAG further extends to uncover a more complete causal graph, i.e., Partial Ancestral Graph, by iterating over the target variables and actively seeking new high-level variables. Moreover, the reliable CD capabilities of COAT also extend the debiased causal inference to unstructured data by discovering an adjustment set. We establish theoretical guarantees for the CD results and verify their efficiency and reliability across realistic benchmarks and real-world case studies.

papers.title: Faithful Federated Tabular Data Synthesis
papers.abstract: Synthetic data is an important data source in the AI era. This paper studies the generation of mixed-type tabular synthetic data in federated settings, where two key challenges arise: ensuring distributional fidelity and effectively handling mixed-type data. We propose Federated Integrative Two-Step Synthesis (FITS), a framework for mixed-type tabular data synthesis. At its core is a two-step federated algorithm for estimating conditional cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) using local linear regression. Building on this algorithm, we develop a federated synthesis procedure based on the probability chain rule to ensure distributional fidelity. To handle mixed-type data, FITS introduces a continualization method that lifts discrete variables into a continuous space and recovers their discrete distributions without loss at both the density-function and CDF levels. This transformation provides a unified continuous representation of mixed-type variables, facilitating the application of local linear regression and synthetic data generation. Our theoretical analysis characterizes the conditional density and cumulative distribution functions of the continualized mixed-type variables and establishes the uniform convergence of the resulting federated conditional CDF estimators. Experiments demonstrate that FITS-generated synthetic data improves downstream task performance for all clients, with the benefits depending on how the synthetic data is used.

papers.title: Not All Mislabels Are Equal: Efficient Task-Aware Auditing with Confidence Sequences
papers.abstract: We study efficient, adaptive auditing of categorical labels in a fixed dataset, motivated by biodiversity-credit programs in which expert verification of species records is costly and downstream scores (e.g., payment) are more sensitive to errors on certain labels than on others. Our proposed ATLAS framework couples anytime-valid inference with a task-aware adaptive auditing policy. Representing label corrections through a confusion matrix, we prioritize which data points to inspect next based on both label uncertainty and the influence of potential label corrections on the downstream score function. For linear scores such as the mislabel rate, our priority-aware approach certifies the overall label error rate to $\pm 2$ percentage points with 24% and 11% fewer audits than random sampling on biodiversity data from Kenya and a widely used CIFAR-10N benchmark, respectively. For nonlinear scores such as the Hill-Shannon diversity, we exploit a linear-envelope representation that reduces inference to a family of linear-score audits; priority-aware sampling reaches the target precision with 36% fewer audits. When distribution-free guarantees are prohibitively costly, we develop a model-based Bayesian alternative that trades assumption-free validity for substantially fewer audits. Our biodiversity case study highlights a gap between statistical validity and practical feasibility: generic methods such as Serfling's bound and existing confidence-sequence procedures are rigorous but can require prohibitively many expert reviews in practice. Together, these results show task-aware auditing can significantly reduce the number of expert audits needed while providing finite-sample, anytime-valid guarantees.

papers.title: Synthetic Data Augmentation for Functional Data: Wasserstein Risk Bounds and Diffusion-Based Conditional Generation
papers.abstract: Functional data are costly to collect; samples of tens to hundreds of curves are common. Synthetic data augmentation can help, but its theory is developed for finite-dimensional data and relies on total variation, which is uninformative for functions. We study augmentation with a class-conditional functional diffusion generator and state guarantees in the Wasserstein-1 distance. For stable downstream estimators, we bound the risk of training on synthetic curves, from above and below, by the risk of training on as many real curves plus a generation penalty, and derive the best number of synthetic curves and a condition under which synthetic data outperform real data. For allocating synthetic curves under class imbalance, we bound the excess risk of training on real and synthetic curves together, without sample splitting. In applications to temperature, hyperspectral and gait curves, augmentation improved classification, function-to-scalar regression and function-to-function regression, and directing synthetic curves to the minority class gave the largest gain under class imbalance.

papers.title: Pro-Active Inference
papers.abstract: Estimating a population mean is fundamental across scientific applications, but observing every outcome can be prohibitively expensive. Often, covariates and machine learning (ML) predictions are available for the full population, even when only a small subset of outcomes can be observed. How can we leverage this information to proactively select observations to label, update ML predictions as labels arrive, and construct statistically valid confidence intervals? We develop a general, without-replacement formulation of Pro-Active Inference (PAI), extending our earlier with-replacement approach and building on Active Statistical Inference. Rather than making fixed-order label-skip decisions, PAI proactively selects which observation to label next from the remaining covariate pool while accommodating online ML updates. We establish PAI's finite-sample unbiasedness and asymptotic validity, develop an improved finite-sample variance estimator, and extend PAI to superpopulation inference without Bonferroni corrections or $\alpha$-splitting. We characterize PAI's potential efficiency gains over Batch Active Inference in a quasi-oracle setting, highlighting the role of prediction-residual imbalance. Across eight diverse datasets, PAI achieves greater sampling efficiency than Sequential Active Inference in the vast majority of tested settings with near-nominal statistical coverage, using the same ML predictor and uncertainty score. However, comparisons with simpler baselines such as Prediction-Powered Inference and uniform sampling, as well as the closely related Prediction-Powered Active Testing, reveal when additional adaptivity helps or hurts statistical efficiency. Through interpretable, theory-motivated diagnostics and frozen-ML ablations, we investigate when and why PAI gains or loses efficiency, highlighting the initial residual-estimation problem and subsequent online learning dynamics.

papers.title: Causal Inference Under Unmeasured Confounding With Negative Controls: A Minimax Learning Approach
papers.abstract: We study the estimation of causal parameters when not all confounders are observed and instead negative controls are available. Recent work has shown how these can enable identification and efficient estimation via two so-called bridge functions. In this paper, we tackle the primary challenges in causal inference with negative controls: identifying and estimating these bridge functions. Previous work has typically relied on completeness conditions for identification, imposed uniqueness assumptions for estimation, and focused on parametric models for the bridge functions. Instead, we provide an alternative identification strategy that assumes the existence of two bridge functions rather than completeness conditions. We also provide new estimators for these functions based on minimax learning formulations. These estimators accommodate general function classes such as Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces and neural networks. We study finite-sample convergence results both for estimating bridge functions themselves and for the final estimation of the causal parameter under a variety of combinations of assumptions. We avoid uniqueness conditions on the bridge functions as much as possible.

papers.title: Computationally efficient goodness-of-fit tests through kernelized Stein discrepancy
papers.abstract: Models with intractable normalizing constants are widely used in statistics and machine learning. Assessing the adequacy of such models poses significant challenges: obtaining samples from the fitted model often requires sophisticated sampling algorithms. Moreover, model fitting sometimes requires iterative numerical optimization, making bootstrap procedures that require repeated refitting computationally expensive. In this paper, we leverage the kernel-based testing framework to develop a general semiparametric goodness-of-fit test based on the kernelized Stein discrepancy. We establish the consistency and the asymptotic null distribution of the test statistic under general nuisance estimation. To produce a level-$\alpha$ test, we propose a novel influence-adjusted wild bootstrap that requires neither refitting the model nor sampling from it. We prove the consistency of the proposed bootstrap test procedure under the null and the alternative, and characterize its limiting power under contiguous local alternatives. Across simulations ranging from classical normality testing to models with intractable likelihoods, the proposed test delivers competitive or superior power at a computational cost orders of magnitude lower than that of existing approaches. We illustrate the method by assessing the adequacy of a protein signaling network model for reverse-phase protein array data from lung adenocarcinoma tumors. As a complementary insight, we show that the SKSD test can be regarded as a nonparametric score test under exponentially tilted models, connecting score-based and distance-based goodness-of-fit testing.

papers.title: Multi-Domain Empirical Bayes for Linearly-Mixed Causal Representations
papers.abstract: Causal representation learning (CRL) aims to learn low-dimensional causal latent variables from high-dimensional observations. While identifiability has been extensively studied for CRL, estimation has been less explored. We use empirical Bayes (EB) to estimate causal representations from multiple domains whose differences reflect interventions in a shared causal model. Multi-domain CRL poses a simultaneous inference problem suited to EB. Here, we propose an EB $f$-modeling algorithm that improves the quality of learned causal variables by exploiting invariant structure within and across domains. Specifically, we consider linear measurement models with interventional priors induced by an acyclic latent causal model with known graph and intervention targets. We develop an EM-style algorithm based on causally structured score matching. In experiments on synthetic and semi-synthetic single-cell data, our proposed method achieves more accurate estimation than alternative methods and baselines.

papers.title: Isotonic Conformal Inference
papers.abstract: A predictor with small overall bias can still exhibit systematic bias conditional on its predicted value, limiting its reliability for downstream uncertainty quantification and candidate screening. We propose Isotonic Conformal Inference, a unified framework for prediction and multiple testing that separates calibration from inference and exploits the level set structure of an isotonic predictor. This structure enables the computation of localized conformal quantiles and $p$-values while avoiding repeated isotonic refitting across candidate responses. For prediction, we introduce Split Isotonic Conformal Prediction (sICP) and Transductive Isotonic Conformal Prediction (tICP), establish prediction-conditional coverage guarantees for both methods, and characterize their finite-sample and asymptotic self-calibration properties. For selection, we introduce Isotonic Conformal Selection (ICS), which provides finite-sample stratum-conditional false discovery rate control. Experiments on simulated regression problems, a healthcare-utilization dataset, and a high-throughput ADMET drug discovery dataset demonstrate the practical performance of the framework and substantially lower computational costs relative to full transductive baselines.

papers.title: Optimal Priors for Betting Tests with Bounded Payoffs: An Exact Expected-Time Characterization
papers.abstract: Testing by betting is a powerful framework that recasts hypothesis testing as a betting game. A popular approach spreads the initial wealth over fixed bets according to a prior distribution, using a universal portfolio algorithm. For suitable priors, this approach achieves the optimal expected rejection time as the error probability goes to zero at a fixed alternative. Yet, priors with this guarantee can behave quite differently near the null. This motivates the question: Which prior should we use in testing-by-betting algorithms? We study bounded scalar payoffs and, under technical conditions, prove a sharp formula for expected rejection time, uniform over all bounded alternatives as the error probability tends to zero. The formula shows how the prior's mass around the zero bet determines the cost of adapting to an unknown alternative. We characterize the priors that attain the best possible leading constant when the error probability and alternative vary together. We also show that no valid test can uniformly improve on this cost across ranges of alternatives near the null. In particular, the uniform prior can require arbitrarily more observations than suitable priors that concentrate around the zero bet. A general inversion argument converts our results into sharp expected times to reach a prescribed confidence-sequence width. We also give a concrete prior choice and an FFT-based algorithm with almost linear computational complexity.

papers.title: Regression Adjustment for Ratios of Treatment Effects in Randomized Experiments
papers.abstract: We study regression adjustment for ratios of treatment effects in completely randomized experiments. The existing literature adjusts the numerator and denominator separately, but this approach misses the efficiency target, loss of which matters more when richer or high-dimensional covariate information and flexible or regularized prediction methods are used to pursue further efficiency gains. We propose a two-step estimator that directly predicts the relevant transformed outcome. Using cross-fitting, our method accommodates high-dimensional first-stage prediction while keeping the final adjustment fixed-dimensional, thereby avoiding instability from a growing number of adjustment covariates. We further develop persistence-based LASSO theory that does not require sparsity, permits more covariates than observations, and allows cross-validated penalty selection under prediction-level conditions. For additional efficiency gains, our augmented two-step estimator nests the benchmark adjustment spaces and is therefore asymptotically no less efficient than the benchmark estimators, while its feasible conservative variance estimator satisfies the same efficiency ordering. Simulation studies and a real-data analysis demonstrate that our proposed estimator performs better than existing methods.

papers.title: Smoothing splines with some discontinuities
authors: Giulio Cesare Gatto Ronchieri (University of Milano-Bicca
papers.abstract: We generalize cubic smoothing splines to signals with a finite number of discontinuities at unknown positions. Rather than changing the roughness penalty, we deform the domain over which it is computed: every interval between consecutive observations can be stretched by a non-negative warp, subject to a total budget, and the optimizer spends the budget only where a jump makes stretching cheaper than bending. The estimator inherits the state-space form of smoothing splines, so it can be fitted by maximum likelihood with the Kalman filter, and it also admits a fast alternating algorithm that solves a banded linear system and takes a projected-gradient step on the warps. The budget is selected by an extended Bayesian information criterion whose constant is calibrated by simulation. In a Monte Carlo comparison the new estimators reconstruct a piecewise-smooth signal more accurately than the cubic smoothing spline with discontinuities of Storath and Weinmann, at the cost of more false alarms. Two energy applications illustrate the method: the temperature response of electricity demand in Northern Italy, and retail fuel prices, whose discontinuities, changes in excise duties, are dated by public record. The three supplements follow the references.

papers.title: Informative inference on the average treatment effect with instrumental variables
papers.abstract: Policy decisions often depend on whether the average treatment effect (ATE) exceeds a specific cutoff. In instrumental variable (IV) settings, point identification of the ATE requires strong assumptions that are often difficult to justify. Therefore, many researchers shift their attention to identification of the local (L) ATE or target bounds of the ATE. Both strategies have well-known drawbacks: the substantive relevance of the LATE is frequently questioned, and the bounds are often too wide to be informative. We propose a simple sensitivity analysis that allows researchers to maintain focus on the ATE, and then discuss its connection to related bounding procedures. Based on these results, researchers can decide, in a principled manner, whether the sign of the ATE is inferable under assumptions they deem credible. The proposed strategies are easy to apply, and we illustrate their value with two real-data examples. The R package ivate implements our procedures.

papers.title: Demand Estimation with Unobserved Stockout Substitution: Exact Likelihood Maximization
papers.abstract: When a product is sold out, customers who prefer it may buy a substitute or leave without purchasing. Efficient demand estimation in this setting is challenging when inventory is observed only at replenishments, because the stockout times, and hence the products available to each customer, are unobserved. Estimating demand efficiently under stockout substitution has been a challenging problem since Anupindi et al. (1998), and it has become more pressing as the scale of such problem instances grows thanks to innovations in retailing such as unmanned stores. We provide a complete solution to this problem for the multinomial logit (MNL) model, the most widely used model of customer choice. Using a continuous-time representation of the purchase process developed in Zhou et al. (2026), we show that the exact likelihood and its gradient are one-dimensional integrals, no matter how many products, customers, or stockouts there are. Both can be evaluated at a cost linear in the numbers of products and periods. Our method estimates demand for 2,000 products from 2,000 selling periods in under ten minutes.

papers.title: Adequacy radii for stepped-wedge trials with time-varying effects
papers.abstract: Complete stepped-wedge designs guarantee eventual intervention delivery, but their final periods contain no concurrent controls. Under exposure-time heterogeneity this creates a design-analysis tension: a constant-effect analysis can be precise while targeting a design-dependent contrast, whereas an exposure-time indicator (ETI) analysis targets a prespecified time-averaged effect but may be much less precise. We develop an adequacy radius that quantifies the size of exposure-time heterogeneity compatible with a prespecified tolerance for estimand mismatch, and combine it with precision calculations to compare complete wedges with rollout-constrained hybrid designs that retain a wait-list arm. For a balanced wedge with a wait-list under the Hussey-Hughes model, the wait-list share and the correlation act on the constant-effect GLS estimand through a single scalar; we prove that the radius increases strictly with the wait-list share and decreases strictly with the within-cluster correlation, but remains bounded. Numerical optimisation and a model-based redesign of a weekend allied-health trial show that intermediate hybrids make estimand-aligned ETI analysis materially more affordable, giving a robustness-precision frontier rather than a binary choice between a complete wedge and a parallel trial. A second trial, of digital adherence support for tuberculosis treatment, has the same radius but no detectable heterogeneity; its test of a constant effect would detect heterogeneity large enough to halve the coverage of the nominal interval only 37% of the time. The contribution is a diagnostic and design principle: when exposure-time heterogeneity is plausible, retaining concurrent controls reduces the price of analysing the estimand one intends to report.

papers.title: Optimal tradeoffs between variance and sensitivity, via Hellinger-Kantorovich geometry
papers.abstract: While the goal of classical statistical theory is to minimize the variance of unbiased estimators, an additional goal of some recent research is to minimize or constrain other notions of the instability of estimators. In particular, a subset of the authors recently introduced a notion of instability termed "sensitivity", which represents the expected amount that an estimator would change if its inputs were infinitesimally perturbed. In this work, we study the multiobjective problem of minimizing both the variance and sensitivity over unbiased estimators in a given statistical model, and we aim to determine Pareto optimal tradeoffs between these two objectives. Our main results show that the Pareto front for these tradeoffs is precisely determined by endowing the statistical model with the Hellinger-Kantorovich geometry, which interpolates between the Hellinger and Wasserstein geometries that are known to be associated, respectively, with the separate minimization of variance and sensitivity. We also develop a $Z$-estimation technique which constructs estimators that asymptotically achieve Pareto optimal pairs of variance and sensitivity. While computing the Pareto front and constructing the resulting estimators in practice requires solving a continuum of partial differential equations, we fully execute this program in some parametric examples of interest where the analysis is already non-trivial. Our results also shed light on some classical statistical problems, for example by showing that the maximum likelihood estimator achieves the smallest asymptotic sensitivity among all estimators achieving the optimal asymptotic variance.

papers.title: Gini representations of skewness, kurtosis and higher-order moments
papers.abstract: We provide pairwise-difference (Gini-type) representations of higher-order central moments for both general random variables and empirical moments. Such representations do not require a measure of location. For third and fourth moments, this yields pairwise-difference representations of skewness and kurtosis coefficients. We show that all central moments possess such representations, so no reference to the mean is needed for moments of any order. This is done by considering i.i.d. replications of the random variables considered, by observing that central moments can be interpreted as covariances between a random variable and powers of the same variable, and by giving recursions which link the pairwise-difference representation of any moment to lower order ones.

papers.title: Near-boundary asymptotics for profile score statistics
papers.abstract: We establish asymptotic results for profile score statistics under sequences of parameters that may tend to the boundary of the parameter set. When the likelihood is profiled over a set with boundary points, the distribution of the statistic can depend, even asymptotically, on a distance to the boundary that cannot be estimated consistently. We address this in three ways. First, we give conditions under which the nuisance score has a root on an extended parameter set, and the profile score statistic formed with that root converges to a chi-squared distribution. Second, we show that the efficient score statistic converges to a chi-squared distribution under a separate condition that can hold even for estimators constrained to the original set. Both lead to confidence regions with asymptotically correct coverage probability, uniformly on sets that may contain boundary points, and the conditions allow the scores for the interest and nuisance parameters to grow at different rates or become asymptotically collinear. Third, we quantify the coverage error of applying the profile score statistic without an extended set. We approximate the distribution of the statistic and bound the error by a quantity that decays like a normal tail in the standardized distance to the boundary. The approximation also gives one-sided tests with least favorable critical values whose asymptotic size is at most the nominal level. We illustrate the results in a zero-inflated Poisson model and a one-way random effects model.

papers.title: Recursive moment updates for scalable Bayesian nonparametric regression
papers.abstract: Bayesian nonparametric regression methods have wide applications in statistics and machine learning, but inference can often be expensive or require approximations. This paper introduces a class of recursive moment function updates which are closed form, interpretable, expedient, and fully quantify Bayesian uncertainty through the martingale posterior. The proposed recursive updates can be used off-the-shelf and encompass challenging scenarios such as nonparametric heteroscedasticity, heavy-tailed or skewed noise, and importantly generalize to the multi-output case with missing outcomes without any significant loss in tractability or speed. We show frequentist consistency under weak assumptions in the aforementioned scenarios, and demonstrate empirically that our proposed method is orders of magnitude faster than competing Bayesian nonparametric approaches, with competitive or even superior prediction and estimation accuracy.

papers.title: Identification and curvature bias for shared inputs in multichannel dynamical models
papers.abstract: Pooling many channels with a shared unknown input can leave persistent bias when each channel retains a fixed number of observations and its own incidental parameters. For heterogeneous smooth channel manifolds under isotropic noise, the second-order bias is an information-weighted regression of mean curvature on normal input velocity. A feasible correction gives centred Gaussian inference as the noise level $\sigma$ decreases with $R\sigma^6\to0$, compared with $R\sigma^2\to0$ without correction. We extend the stochastic expansion and studentization to deterministic channel arrays with densely correlated Gaussian errors of bounded covariance operator norm. General marginal covariance adds a forcing term that can bias even flat channels, while cross-channel covariance changes uncertainty. For Gaussian errors with a separable frame-by-channel covariance whose channel factor is autoregressive in a known ordering, an independent zero-mean calibration field yields a covariance estimator accurate enough for corrected inference. Boundary accumulation and fixed working population models introduce distinct bias terms; rational-multiplier and zero-count arguments connect identification to frame-integrated compartment models. Simulations test both oracle and estimated-covariance inference, including independent PET replications. Moderate-noise undercoverage, optimization ambiguity and the need to validate reconstruction covariance limit practical inference. The real-data example supports sensitivity analysis, not clinically calibrated intervals.

papers.title: Renewable model averaging for generalized linear models
papers.abstract: Prediction is one of the most important research topics in statistics and machine learning. Moreover, in the domain of streaming data analysis, real-time prediction has become a rapidly growing research field in recent years, owing to the abundance of streaming data. In many fields of scientific research, such as biomedical research, weather forecasting, and traffic management, improving real-time prediction of streaming data is crucial in general. However, the complicated features of streaming data, such as large-scale and high-velocity, impose both theoretical and computational challenges to the development and evaluation of real-time prediction in this field, especially when the investigator has multiple models at hand. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel Renewable Model Averaging method through Quadratic approximation (ReMAQ) for generalized linear model (GLM) for streaming data. By approximating the model averaging procedure for GLMs (which is typically a convex optimization problem) with a quadratic optimization formulation, ReMAQ allows us to update the model averaging prediction sequentially when a new batch of data arrives, without accessing the entire historical data. Moreover, ReMAQ is also computationally efficient as one only needs to consider a quadratic programming problem in each steps of updating. Under certain regular conditions, we also show that the proposed ReMAQ weight is asymptotically equivalent to that by the oracle model averaging based on the inaccessible full data, the asymptotic optimality of ReMAQ is then established accordingly. The proposed method is also assessed by simulation studies. We apply our proposed ReMAQ in the study of the Airline On-Time Performance Dataset and the results demonstrate the superiority our method in practical situations.

papers.title: An Integrated Framework for Assessing Interpretability in Exploratory Factor Analysis
papers.abstract: Interpretability in Exploratory Factor Analysis is characterized by the fundamental trade-off between structural sparseness and explained common variance. Lacking formal evaluation metrics, researchers frequently sacrifice parsimony in the pattern matrix to maximize the model's explanatory coverage. For this reason, we extend Hoyer's sparseness ratio into a flexible \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal{L}_{p_1}/\mathcal{L}_{p_2}$}{Lp1/Lp2} formulation to introduce the Interpretability Index $I$, defined as the geometric mean of explained common variance and the generalized sparseness index. We analyze the asymptotic behavior of $I$ as norm orders increase, establishing that raising $p_2$ alone yields a stable limit, whereas increasing $p_1$ and $p_2$ jointly causes the measure to saturate. The canonical choice $(p_1,p_2)=(2,4)$ balances numerical stability with a smooth, tractable objective. We finally demonstrate, on five benchmark datasets from the statistical literature, how the Interpretability Index provides a systematic criterion for selecting the optimal parametrization of the latent space according to the user's analytical goals.

papers.title: Optimal Experimental Design for the Polynomial Maximization Method: a Higher-Order Reserve Beyond Second-Order Design Theory
papers.abstract: Optimal designs for regression with asymmetric errors build on the second-order least squares estimator (SLSE) of Wang and Leblanc (2008), whose gain over ordinary least squares (OLS) comes from the error skewness. With i.i.d. errors the optimally weighted SLSE solves the same estimating equation as the degree-two Polynomial Maximization Method (PMM), a family whose degree-$S$ location estimator has asymptotic variance $g_S\le1$ times that of the sample mean. We derive optimal designs for this family when the errors are independent with constant variance but have standardised cumulants of order three and higher that vary with the regressor (cumulant heteroscedasticity). For a known reduction field $g_S(x)$, the $g_S$-weighted information matrix $M_{g_S}$ obeys the Kiefer-Wolfowitz equivalence theorem. A constant field leaves the OLS-optimal design unchanged; a non-constant field can change it but need not. For symmetric errors with varying kurtosis, the PMM$_2$ and conditional-SLSE designs cannot depart from the OLS-optimal one, whereas a degree-three design can. A stratify-and-pool PMM$_S$ estimator attains $N\mathrm{Cov}(\hat\theta)\to\sigma^2M_{g_S}^{-1}$ at every degree as all strata grow; its per-stratum reduction is below one only for symmetric errors with the symmetry imposed. For a quadratic model on $[0,1]$ with symmetric Beta errors of unit variance and dose-varying shape, the third-order design for the known field has $A$-efficiency $1.047$ relative to the OLS-optimal design, and $1.001$ under the $D$-criterion. A two-stage procedure that estimates the field from a one-third pilot builds designs of $A$-efficiency $1.014$-$1.020$ at $N=600$-$2400$; its realised mean-squared-error ratio against the OLS-optimal design ranges from $0.89$ (a loss) to $1.08$.

papers.title: Extreme proxies for causal identification: deconfounding with outliers
papers.abstract: Causal identification under unobserved confounding typically relies on additional structure, such as a valid instrument or proxy variables. We show that heavy tailed variables offer an alternative route to identification by revealing treatment variation for which confounding becomes asymptotically negligible. Our key assumption is extreme propagation: when an unobserved confounder takes an extreme value, some observed variable in the system (called a safeguard) will become extreme with large probability. This way, selecting extreme treatment observations while safeguards remain non-extreme makes confounding asymptotically negligible relative to the treatment. We call this certification. We derive graphical conditions specifying which latent confounders must be monitored by safeguards and distributional conditions ensuring effective certification. The framework includes valid-instrument and double-proxy structures as special cases, as well as confounded instruments that are invalid in most approaches that do not exploit heavy tails. Geometrically, certification isolates the extremal ray whose slope equals the causal effect. This connects causal identification with multivariate extreme-value geometry and motivates a family of novel simple estimators. Simulations demonstrate performance gains under nonlinear confounding and heavy tails, while revealing limitations in light-tailed regimes (where cancellation can conceal extreme confounding from the safeguards). We validate our methodology in simulation studies and by recovering the ground-truth flow in a river discharge application.

papers.title: Nonlinear Reduced-Bias Extreme Value Index Estimators: A Comparative Study
papers.abstract: The estimation of the extreme value index (EVI) plays a central role in extreme value theory (EVT), particularly in the statistical modelling of heavy-tailed phenomena. Classical semi-parametric estimators of the EVI are known to suffer from substantial bias, especially for moderate sample sizes and for common choices of the number of upper order statistics. In recent years, several reduced-bias (RB) methodologies have been proposed in order to improve finite-sample performance while preserving asymptotic efficiency. In this paper, we present new classes of nonlinear RB EVI-estimators based on power mean-type and Lehmer mean-type functionals of upper log-excesses. Under a unified higher-order framework, asymptotic representations are derived and bias and variance properties are compared relative to other RB EVI classes introduced in the literature. An asymptotic comparison at optimal levels is conducted to identify regions of the space parameter where the proposed estimators are more efficient. A comprehensive Monte Carlo simulation study assesses the finite sample behaviour of the new estimators for several heavy tailed models. The results show that nonlinear reduced-bias estimators can provide improvements in bias and root mean squared error, although their relative performance depends on the underlying distribution and the choice of the tuning parameter. An application to hydrological data illustrates their practical use and the importance of threshold selection in EVI estimation.

papers.title: Inference for Causal Path-Specific Effects in Longitudinal Studies with Repeated Treatments and Multiple Mediators
papers.abstract: In longitudinal studies, repeated treatments may be followed by different sequences of mediators and time-varying covariates. We develop semiparametric inference for path-specific effects in this setting, allowing the number, type, and ordering of intermediate variables to vary across treatment occasions. Under consistency, positivity, edge consistency, and the cross-world restrictions of a nonparametric structural equation model with independent errors, path-specific means are identified by the edge g-formula. We derive two parameterizations of the efficient influence function of the identifying functional. The first follows the observed-data factorization and uses conditional intermediate-variable densities. The second uses sequential regressions to replace the corresponding integrations and Bayes' rule to express density ratios through treatment-history regressions, thereby avoiding direct estimation of intermediate-variable densities. Each yields a one-step estimator that permits flexible nuisance estimation. We establish product-rate conditions for asymptotic linearity and semiparametric efficiency. The density-based estimator has blockwise multiple robustness, generalizing triply robust estimation, while the regression-based estimator has sequential multiple robustness. We further develop a sensitivity analysis for selected violations of cross-world independence assumptions used to identify these effects. Simulations examine finite-sample performance and robustness to model misspecifications. An application to the Framingham Heart Study examines sustained-smoking effects on systolic blood pressure along pathways through repeated body mass index measurements. The proposed methods are implemented in the R package flexPaths on Gihub at xxou/flexPaths.

papers.title: A new categorical correlation measure
papers.abstract: Feature screening in high-dimensional classification is an important problem in statistical learning, particularly in genomics, imaging, and other scientific fields, especially when the number of predictors exceeds the sample size. Zhong et al. (2024) present a semi-distance covariance (SDCov) as a dependence measure between a categorical random variable and a multivariate continuous random vector, presenting it as a promising tool for group-wise feature screening. However, SDCov is defined using the Euclidean norm, and its performance may be affected when the data is derived from heavy-tailed distributions or when outlier observations are present, which is a common phenomenon in high-dimensional data. This study proposes a modification of SDCov by replacing the $L_2$ norm with an $L_1$ norm. This adjustment results in a dependency measure between a categorical variable and a multivariate continuous variable that maintains the independence-characterization property of the original definition. Additionally, it serves as a robust and interpretable measure, particularly in the presence of outliers in the data. We establish the fundamental theoretical properties of the proposed measure and introduce a U-statistics-based estimator along with JEL-based inference for the measure. Additionally, we have introduced a test for independence based on the proposed measure. An extensive Monte Carlo simulation is performed to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed measure in comparison to existing measures in the literature. The proposed measure is applied in feature screening, as illustrated with the ADNI Alzheimer's disease dataset and the Iris dataset. The data analysis shows the proposed measure's effectiveness in identifying variables that facilitate strong class separation of the respective response variables.

papers.title: Distribution-free predictive inference with instrumental variables
papers.abstract: We study the problem of predictive inference with outcomes missing not at random, when instrumental variables are available. While conformal prediction and weighted conformal prediction provide valid distribution-free inference when outcomes are missing completely at random and missing at random, respectively, inference is generally not possible without additional assumptions when outcomes are missing not at random. In this work, we consider a setting where we remain within the distribution-free framework but instead have access to an instrumental variable (IV). We explore the theoretical possibility of IV predictive inference and establish that it is characterized by a parameter that we refer to as the identification index. We derive an impossibility result for the case where the identification index is not sufficiently large, showing that any distribution-free approach fails to provide informative inference in this case. For the case where the identification index is sufficiently large, we introduce a practical method that achieves informative predictive inference. Our method leverages modern semiparametric efficiency theory which involves deriving the efficient influence function of the identifying functional for sharp IV bounds of the quantiles of the missing outcome, delivering a double robustness property in the coverage guarantee of the proposed framework for IV-based predictive inference. We illustrate the theoretical results and the performance of the proposed procedure through simulations and two real-data applications---FES wages and NHANES III self-reported heights.

papers.title: Recertifying decisions via e-closure: uniform improvements of conformal risk control and randomized e-BH
papers.abstract: Statistical procedures often control expected loss at a prescribed level while leaving part of their risk budget unused. Building on the e-value representation of risk-controlled decisions and the e-closure principle for multiple testing, we formulate recertification, a general paradigm for improving procedures by exploiting computable slack in their validity certificates. A valid procedure's losses normalized by their risk budgets form a state-indexed e-value collection; conversely, decisions whose normalized losses are bounded by this collection inherit its risk guarantees. Recertification uses distributional structure to quantify slack, enlarge the certifying e-values while preserving validity, and construct less conservative decisions. We develop two applications. For conformal risk control (CRC) with a known loss family, recertification redistributes unused risk budget among the held-out points of each hypothetical augmented sample. The resulting controller is valid under every finite exchangeable law and no more conservative than CRC on any calibration sample. For convex losses on an interval of actions, repeated recertification converges geometrically to an admissible controller. For false discovery rate control with arbitrarily dependent e-values, recertification exploits unused conditional budgets in randomized e-BH. It yields a closed-form randomized procedure whose rejection set contains that of randomized e-BH for every realization of the shared randomization and whose expected number of rejections is maximal subject to the same conditional budget constraints. Recertifying with the larger e-collection of closed e-BH gives a second closed-form procedure whose rejection set contains that of the first. Experiments on CIFAR-100 hierarchical classification and multiple testing simulations demonstrate improved budget utilization, informativeness and power over the baselines.
